title: Hash Tables From Scratch: Collisions, Load Factor and Amortized Resizing
description: A from-scratch explanation of hash tables: hashing, collisions, chaining vs. open addressing, load factor, and the amortized analysis that makes doubling the table cost O(1) per insert.

content.authorization_basis: Original synthetic transcript authored for the AI Video Discovery project. No real video exists.

segments.text: In this video I want to explain how a hash table works under the hood, and specifically answer a question that bugged me for years.
If resizing a hash table means copying everything, how can inserts possibly be constant time? Let's build it up from scratch.
A hash table is an array of slots, usually called buckets, plus a hash function.
The hash function takes a key, say the string apple, and turns it into an integer.
You take that integer modulo the number of buckets, and that gives you an index. Store the value there.
To look it up later, hash the key again, land on the same index, done. No scanning.
The problem is collisions.
Two different keys can land on the same bucket, and with any realistic amount of data they will.
By the birthday paradox,
with three hundred and sixty-five buckets you only need about twenty-three keys before there's a better than even chance of a collision.
So collisions aren't an edge case. They're the normal case, and the design question is how to handle them.
There are two main families. The first is separate chaining.
Each bucket holds a small list, and colliding keys just get appended to that list.
Lookup hashes to the bucket and then walks the list. The second is open addressing.
Everything lives directly in the array, and if your slot is taken, you probe for another one.
The simplest version is linear probing. Try the next slot, then the next.
Linear probing is very cache-friendly, because you're walking through adjacent memory, but it suffers from clustering.
Occupied runs grow, and long runs attract more keys, which makes them longer still.
Either way, performance depends on the load factor, which is the number of stored keys divided by the number of buckets.
If the load factor stays bounded, say below three quarters, the expected length of a chain or a probe sequence stays bounded too,
assuming the hash function spreads keys out reasonably evenly. That's where the constant-time claim comes from.
It's expected constant time, and it rests on two assumptions, a decent hash function and a bounded load factor.
To keep the load factor bounded as you insert, you have to grow the table.
When it gets too full, you allocate a new array, typically twice the size, and re-insert every key,
because each key's index depends on the table size. That single resize is expensive.
If there are n keys, it costs order n. So here's the puzzle.
How is insert constant time if some inserts cost n? The answer is amortized analysis. Let's count.
Suppose you start with one bucket and double every time you fill up.
Resizes happen at sizes one, two, four, eight, and so on up to n.
The total copying work is one plus two plus four, all the way up to n, which is less than two n.
Spread across n inserts, that's fewer than two extra copies per insert. Constant. The doubling is the key.
If you grew by a fixed amount instead, say ten slots each time, you'd resize about n over ten times, each costing up to n,
and the total would be quadratic. Growing geometrically is what makes the expensive operation rare enough to pay for itself.
Two practical notes. First, amortized constant is not the same as worst-case constant.
An individual insert can still stall while the table resizes, which matters in latency-sensitive systems.
Some implementations resize incrementally, moving a few buckets on each operation, to spread that cost out.
Second, the hash function matters for security, not just speed.
If an attacker can predict your hash function, they can send keys that all collide, turning every lookup into a linear scan.
That's why many languages now seed their string hashing with a random value per process. Summary.
Buckets plus a hash function. Collisions handled by chaining or probing. Load factor kept bounded by geometric resizing.
And amortized analysis explains why the occasional expensive resize still averages out to constant time.
In the next video, I'll implement this in about sixty lines and we'll measure it.
